name: Louis XVI of France
summary: King of France from 1774 to 1792, Louis defended hereditary monarchy, royal participation in lawmaking, and protection of property. His Edict of Versailles recognized the civil status of non-Catholics while reserving public worship to Catholicism. He approved a military alliance with the United States and later used his royal veto against the deportation of non-juring priests.

property-fundamental.rationale: The 23 June 1789 declaration says all property rights, without exception, shall be constantly respected, including tithes and feudal and seigniorial rights.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Edict of Versailles reserved public worship to Catholicism, gave Catholic rites legal effect in civil registration and restricted access to offices carrying religious duties.

open-borders.rationale: Louis’s 1777 declaration restricted entry into metropolitan France on racial grounds and ordered the removal of people who entered in violation of the prohibition.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The June 1791 declaration defends a king with legislative and military powers, and the will advises a reigning successor. Neither addresses a ceremonial monarchy.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Louis’s June 1789 program made tax and administrative reforms while explicitly preserving the existing orders and their constitutional role.

notes: This pass searched royal declarations and correspondence, parliamentary records, the peace and alliance record, criminal procedure, the legal status of religious and racial minorities, provincial administration, marriage and family law, and grain, coinage and tax policy. For the widest dividing lines, the evidence on the eighteenth-century grain trade and provincial administration did not establish positions on industrial civilization, ethnonationalism, supranational integration or ethnic territorial autonomy. The forest administration proposal and the economic measures reviewed yielded no position on the specific ecology or technology questions. Louis personally accepted the 1791 Constitution as a whole, explained that decision to his brothers as a way to avert civil war, and exercised particular powers under it. Its individual provisions are not attributed to him without evidence that he drove or exercised them. Gutenberg search results were works by other authors. Follow-up on the widest remaining lines compared the 1787 provincial-assembly reforms with the revolutionary departmental settlement, checked the Edict of Versailles against the timing of the September 1792 divorce law, and traced the 1786 Anglo-French commercial negotiations and the 1790 return provision for Protestant exiles. A bilateral trade agreement and a general constitutional acceptance do not establish Louis’s personal answers on protective tariffs, supranational authority or ethnic territorial autonomy. Louis’s June 1791 criticism of the many tiers of local administration was checked against his June 1789 proposal to devolve specified services to provincial assemblies. These sources address the allocation of particular responsibilities without settling a general right of secession or territorial autonomy for an ethnic minority.
